text: Basic Authentication is the simplest way to authenticate an outbound REST Message, and the first real security tradeoff this course asks you to understand: simple to set up, but rarely enough on its own for a production integration.

Basic Auth joins a username and password with a colon, base64-encodes the result, and sends it on the Authorization header of every single request, prefixed with the word Basic. ServiceNow's Authentication Profile builds that header automatically the moment you supply a username and password — your script never touches the raw encoding directly.

Here's the detail that trips people up: base64 is a reversible encoding scheme, not encryption. Anyone who intercepts that header can decode it straight back to the real username and password in one line of code, with no key and no computation beyond a standard library call. The only thing actually protecting a Basic Auth credential in transit is the HTTPS connection underneath it. Send that same header over plain HTTP, and it is effectively plaintext on the wire.

Even running correctly over HTTPS, Basic Auth has three structural weaknesses production integrations care about. First, the real username and password travel on every single request, for as long as the integration runs, instead of a short-lived token obtained once and reused. Second, there's no built-in expiration or rotation — a compromised credential stays valid until a human manually changes it. Third, revocation is blunt: it usually means changing one shared service account's password, which can quietly break every other integration still depending on that same credential.

None of that makes Basic Auth useless. It's still the fastest Authentication Profile to configure for a quick internal test, a sandbox instance, or a legacy external API that genuinely offers nothing stronger. The honest rule this lesson leaves you with: reach for Basic Auth when speed matters more than production rigor, and plan to replace it before the integration goes live against a partner or vendor that actually supports something better.

Basic Auth is simple, but its weaknesses are real: credentials on every request, no expiration, and revocation that can take down more than you intended. Next up: OAuth 2.0 — the approach ServiceNow actually builds its production Authentication Profiles around, and the one that handles tokens for you automatically.
